context.heading: Blessings in the heavenly realms
context.body: Epouranios ("heavenly") appears five times in Ephesians (1:3, 20; 2:6; 3:10; 6:12). It describes the unseen realm where Christ reigns at God's right hand and where hostile powers still operate. Believers already hold every blessing there, real now even though not yet fully visible.

context.heading: Everything summed up in Christ
context.body: Anakephalaioō ("bring together") meant to sum up, as an accountant totals a column or a speaker recaps an argument. It also echoes kephalē ("head"), which Paul uses in verse 22. God's plan is to gather the whole fractured universe, heaven and earth, into coherence under Christ.

context.heading: A deposit on the inheritance
context.body: Arrabōn ("pledge") was a business word for a first installment that guaranteed the rest would be paid. In modern Greek a related word means an engagement ring. The Holy Spirit is God's down payment: a real share of the age to come now, and a promise that the full inheritance is coming.

theology.title: Father, Son and Spirit in one song
theology.body: Verses 3 to 14 move from the Father who chose, to the Son who redeemed, to the Spirit who seals. Each section closes with a refrain: "to the praise of His glory" (vv. 6, 12, 14). Salvation is the work of the whole Trinity, and its goal is God's glory.

theology.title: Chosen in Christ before the world
theology.body: Paul praises God for choosing His people in Christ before the foundation of the world (v. 4). Christians differ on how election relates to human choice, some stressing God's sovereign decree and others His foreknowledge. All agree that salvation starts with God's initiative and rests on Christ, not on our merit.

theology.title: The power that raised Jesus
theology.body: Paul prays they will know the power that raised Christ and seated Him at God's right hand (vv. 19–20). He echoes Psalm 110:1 and Psalm 8:6, with all things placed under His feet. That same resurrection power is at work toward believers now.

application.title: Praise before requests
application.body: Paul spends twelve verses blessing God before he asks for anything. Most of our prayers start with the list of needs and end before praise ever arrives.
application.question: If your prayers this week were written down, how many lines would come before the first request?

application.title: Identity before activity
application.body: Chapters 1 to 3 contain almost no commands; they tell you who you already are in Christ. Much exhausted Christian activity is an attempt to earn what this chapter says has been given.
application.question: What would you stop trying to prove if you believed you already had every spiritual blessing?

context.heading: The ruler of the air
context.body: Many ancient people pictured the air between earth and the heavens as the realm of spirits. Paul speaks the language of a city steeped in magic (Acts 19:19) to say that a real evil ruler (archōn) works in those who disobey God. Sin is not only personal weakness; it has a spiritual power behind it.

context.heading: From resident aliens to citizens
context.body: Paroikos ("foreigner") was a legal term for a resident alien, someone who lived in a city without a citizen's rights. Greek cities guarded citizenship jealously. Paul says Gentile believers are now sympolitēs ("fellow citizens") and even members of God's household, moving from tolerated outsiders to family.

context.heading: The stone that sets the building
context.body: Akrogōniaios ("cornerstone") comes from Isaiah 28:16, where God lays a tested, precious stone in Zion. The cornerstone was laid first and aligned the whole structure. Some scholars think it means a capstone at the top, but either way Christ holds the building together.

theology.title: But God, rich in mercy
theology.body: After three verses describing death in sin, verse 4 turns on two words: "But God." He acts because He is rich in mercy and loves with great love, as He revealed Himself to Moses (Exodus 34:6). Salvation starts in God's character, not in any spark of life in us.

theology.title: Christ is our peace
theology.body: Paul echoes Isaiah 57:19: "peace, peace to those far and near." Through the cross Christ reconciles both Jews and Gentiles to God and to each other in one body (vv. 14–17). Peace is not first a feeling; it is a person who has ended hostility.

theology.title: God moving in
theology.body: From Eden to the tabernacle to Solomon's temple, Scripture tells of God choosing to dwell among His people. Now He builds a temple out of people, Jews and Gentiles together, a dwelling place by His Spirit (vv. 21–22). The church is where God lives.

application.title: Dead, not just struggling
application.body: Paul does not call people without Christ weak or confused but dead. That changes how we see our own conversion and the people we pray for: they need resurrection, not just advice.
application.question: Do you treat the people you pray for as needing better arguments or as needing God to raise them to life?

application.title: The wall you would rebuild
application.body: Christ tore down the dividing wall, yet believers keep rebuilding smaller ones: worship style, politics, class, neighborhood. Each wall says some of the household are less welcome.
application.question: Which kind of Christian would you secretly prefer to keep on the other side of a wall?

application.title: Work prepared in advance
application.body: God prepared good works for His people before they arrived. That includes the coworker who needs patience and the neighbor who needs a ride.
application.question: What ordinary task this week might God have prepared for you before you ever got there?

context.heading: Prisoner of Christ, not of Rome
context.body: Paul was likely under house arrest in Rome, chained to a guard (Acts 28:16, 30). Yet he calls himself the desmios ("prisoner") of Christ Jesus, not of Nero. Ancient readers saw chains as shame; Paul reframes them as service for the Gentiles he is writing to.

context.heading: Riches beyond tracking
context.body: Anexichniastos ("unsearchable") is built on ichnos, a footprint: something whose trail cannot be followed to its end. The Greek Old Testament uses it for God's works (Job 5:9). In the same verse Paul invents a word, "less than the least," a comparative of a superlative, to describe himself.

context.heading: Many-colored wisdom
context.body: Polypoikilos ("manifold") means richly varied, a word used for embroidered cloth or many-colored flowers. Through a church where Jews and Gentiles, rich and poor share one table, God displays His wisdom to the powers in the heavenly realms. The church is meant to be a living tapestry.

theology.title: The God who reveals in His time
theology.body: The promise to Abraham always included the nations. What stayed hidden was the shape of it: Gentiles as equal members of one body, sharing the promise in Christ (vv. 5–6). God keeps His purposes until the right moment and then makes them plain.

theology.title: Father of every family
theology.body: Paul kneels before the Father (patēr), from whom every family (patria) in heaven and on earth is named (vv. 14–15). The wordplay shows God is the original Father, not a projection of human fathers. Every family takes its meaning from Him.

theology.title: Able to do far more
theology.body: The doxology praises God as able to do immeasurably more than all we ask or imagine (v. 20). His power is already at work within His people. Paul's prayers are large because his view of God is larger.

application.title: Your hardship, their courage
application.body: Paul tells the Ephesians not to lose heart over his sufferings, because they are for their glory. How believers handle hardship can strengthen or shake the faith of people watching.
application.question: Whose faith might be shaped by how you handle the hardship you are in right now?

application.title: Known in theory, not in experience
application.body: Paul prays they will know a love that surpasses knowledge. It is possible to explain Christ's love well and still live as if it is not true of you.
application.question: Do you know more about Christ's love than you have actually let yourself experience?

application.title: Asking too small
application.body: God can do far more than we ask, yet many prayers shrink over time to safe, manageable requests.
application.question: What have you stopped asking God for because you decided it was too big?

context.heading: A victory parade from Psalm 68
context.body: Psalm 68:18 pictures God ascending Zion after battle, leading captives and receiving gifts. Paul has Him giving doma ("gifts") instead, a reading also found in some later Jewish interpretation. Victorious kings shared the spoils; the ascended Christ distributes gifts to His people.

context.heading: Rotten talk
context.body: Sapros ("unwholesome") describes rotten fruit or spoiled fish (Matthew 7:17; 13:48). Rotten words do not stay contained; they spread decay to everyone nearby. Paul's alternative is oikodomē, speech that builds up and gives grace to those who hear.

context.heading: A Spirit who can be grieved
context.body: Lypeō ("grieve") is a personal word: you can anger a force, but you can only grieve a person who loves you. Paul echoes Isaiah 63:10, where Israel rebelled and grieved God's Holy Spirit. The verse also recalls the sealing of 1:13, a mark of belonging, not a reason for fear.

theology.title: One God, one people
theology.body: "One Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all" (vv. 4–6) echoes the Shema of Deuteronomy 6:4. Paul names one Spirit, one Lord and one Father in a single breath. The church's unity is rooted in the unity of the triune God Himself.

theology.title: He descended and ascended
theology.body: Christ descended to "the lower parts of the earth" and ascended above the heavens to fill all things (vv. 9–10). Interpreters differ on the descent: His incarnation, His death and burial, or His coming again by the Spirit. All agree the one who stooped lowest now reigns over all.

application.title: Anger with an expiration date
application.body: Paul allows anger but not anger that outlives the day. Resentment carried past sunset over and over slowly becomes part of who we are.
application.question: What anger have you carried past sunset so often that it now feels like your personality?

application.title: From taking to giving
application.body: The former thief is told to work so he will have something to share. Paul gives work a purpose beyond personal comfort.
application.question: Is the goal of your paycheck only to have enough, or also to have something to give?

application.title: Truth and love together
application.body: Speaking the truth in love is how the body grows up. Under pressure most of us drop one: we either soften the truth or sharpen it without love.
application.question: Which do you usually drop when conversations get tense, the truth or the love?

context.heading: Buying up the moment
context.body: Exagorazō ("redeeming") is a marketplace word: to buy up, to snap up a bargain before it is gone. Its object is kairos ("time"), the opportune moment rather than mere clock time. Because the days are evil, wise people seize each opening for good instead of letting it slip.

context.heading: A life that cannot be saved
context.body: Asōtia ("reckless indiscretion") is built from a- ("not") and sōzō ("save"): a wasteful, unsalvageable way of living. Luke uses the related adverb for the prodigal son's reckless living (Luke 15:13). In Ephesus, drunken festivals honored Dionysus, the god of wine; Paul offers the Spirit instead.

context.heading: A household code with a difference
context.body: Greek writers such as Aristotle addressed household rules to the male head about ruling wife, children and slaves. Paul speaks to wives, children and slaves directly as moral agents, and asks husbands for self-giving love. Hypotassō ("submit") in verse 21 also supplies the verb for verse 22 in Greek. Christians differ on how mutual submission shapes the roles that follow.

theology.title: Imitators of a holy God
theology.body: "Be imitators of God, as beloved children" (v. 1) echoes the call to be holy as He is holy (Leviticus 11:44). Christ's self-giving is described as a fragrant offering, the language of Israel's sacrifices (Exodus 29:18). God's holiness is seen most clearly in sacrificial love.

theology.title: The Bridegroom who cleanses
theology.body: Christ loved the church, gave Himself for her and washes her to present her radiant (vv. 25–27). The prophets pictured God as a husband who bathed and clothed His bride Israel (Ezekiel 16:8–14). The Old Testament marriage image finds its fulfillment in Christ and His people.

application.title: Gratitude instead of mockery
application.body: Paul's replacement for crude joking is not silence but thanksgiving. Humor built on mocking others is easy; humor built on delight takes more attention.
application.question: What would your humor sound like if gratitude, not mockery, were its raw material?

application.title: Your unplanned minutes
application.body: Redeeming the time applies most to the minutes nobody schedules: the wait in line, the evening scroll, the drive home.
application.question: Where do your unplanned minutes go, and who actually decided that?

application.title: Love that costs the lover
application.body: Christ's love is measured by what He gave up. In marriage and every close relationship, love that never costs anything is probably not the love Paul is describing.
application.question: In your closest relationship, what has your love cost you lately?

context.heading: Fathers with nearly unlimited power
context.body: Roman law gave the father (paterfamilias) sweeping legal authority over his children, even as adults. Into that world Paul says fathers must not parorgizō ("provoke to anger") their children. Instead they are to raise them in the discipline and instruction "of the Lord," shaping authority by Christ's character.

context.heading: Hand-to-hand struggle
context.body: Palē ("struggle") was the word for wrestling, a close-contact sport in Greek gymnasiums. The enemies include kosmokratores ("powers"), a title some ancient texts gave to astral powers that claimed to rule the world. Paul mixes images: the battle is close, personal and against unseen forces.

context.heading: A shield shaped like a door
context.body: Thyreos ("shield") comes from thyra ("door"): the large, long shield of the Roman soldier, about four feet tall. These shields were made of wood covered in leather, and some ancient writers describe soaking them to quench fire arrows. Soldiers could also lock shields side by side, a picture of faith held together.

theology.title: God's own armor
theology.body: Paul's armor comes from Isaiah, where God Himself puts on righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet (Isaiah 59:17), and where the Messiah wears righteousness and faithfulness as a belt (Isaiah 11:5). The feet bringing good news echo Isaiah 52:7. Believers wear armor first worn by God.

theology.title: The Master over every master
theology.body: Paul reminds masters that they and their slaves share one Master in heaven, who shows no favoritism (v. 9). In a society built on rank, God's lordship levels everyone. That truth planted seeds that would later undermine the slavery Paul's world took for granted.

application.title: Not flesh and blood
application.body: Paul names the real enemy as spiritual forces, not people. In family conflict, church disputes or politics, it is easy to aim all our fire at the person in front of us.
application.question: Who have you been treating as the enemy when the real battle is somewhere else?

application.title: Work for an audience of One
application.body: Paul warns against "eye-service," working well only when watched. Doing the job as for the Lord changes the hours when no one is checking.
application.question: How would your work look different during the hours when no one is watching?

application.title: Ask for courage, not only escape
application.body: Chained in prison, Paul asks for prayer to speak boldly, not mainly for release. His request reorders what we usually pray for in hard places.
application.question: When you pray about your hardest situation, are you asking mostly for escape or for courage?
